content: Losartan administration leads to a reduction in plasma aldosterone concentrations. Despite this effect on aldosterone secretion, there is minimal impact on serum potassium levels. In a single-dose study conducted on healthy volunteers, losartan did not alter the glomerular filtration rate, renal plasma flow, or filtration fraction. Similarly, in multiple-dose studies involving hypertensive patients, losartan showed no significant effects on systemic or renal prostaglandin concentrations, fasting triglycerides, total cholesterol, HDL-cholesterol, or fasting glucose levels. The antihypertensive effects of losartan were primarily demonstrated in four placebo-controlled trials lasting 6 to 12 weeks, with dosages ranging from 10 to 150 mg per day. These studies included comparisons of once-daily versus twice-daily dosing regimens (50–100 mg/day), peak and trough effects, and responses based on gender, age, and race. Additional studies evaluated the combination of losartan with hydrochlorothiazide for antihypertensive efficacy. In the four monotherapy trials, 1,075 patients were randomized to various doses of losartan, while 334 patients received a placebo. The 10 mg and 25 mg doses produced some peak effects (notably 6 hours post-dosing) but showed small and inconsistent trough responses (24 hours post-dosing). Higher doses, such as 150 mg, did not demonstrate greater efficacy than the 50–100 mg range. Twice-daily dosing at 50–100 mg/day consistently resulted in larger trough responses compared to once-daily dosing at the same total dose. Peak effects (6 hours post-dosing) were consistently, though moderately, larger than trough effects, with trough-to-peak ratios for systolic and diastolic responses ranging from 50–95% and 60–90%, respectively. Subgroup analyses based on age, gender, and race revealed that men and women, as well as patients above and below 65 years of age, generally exhibited similar responses to losartan. While losartan effectively reduced blood pressure across racial groups, the effect was somewhat attenuated in Black patients, who are typically a low-renin population. The antihypertensive effect of losartan becomes substantially evident within one week of initiation, with maximal effects observed in some studies between 3 to 6 weeks. Long-term follow-up studies (without placebo control) indicated that the blood pressure-lowering effect of losartan was sustained for up to one year. No rebound hypertension was observed following abrupt discontinuation of losartan. Additionally, there was no significant change in average heart rate among losartan-treated patients in controlled trials. In pediatric hypertension, the antihypertensive efficacy of losartan was evaluated in a trial involving 177 hypertensive children aged 6 to 16 years. Patients weighing less than 50 kg received daily doses of 2.5, 25, or 50 mg of losartan, while those weighing 50 kg or more received 5, 50, or 100 mg daily. Children in the lowest dose group were administered losartan in a suspension formulation. Most pediatric participants had hypertension associated with renal or urogenital disease. At baseline, their sitting diastolic blood pressure (SiDBP) exceeded the 95th percentile for their age, gender, and height. After three weeks, losartan reduced systolic and diastolic blood pressure in a dose-dependent manner. However, the lowest dose (0.07 mg/kg) did not consistently demonstrate antihypertensive efficacy.
